opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think fab capacity is one of the more important constraints to think about, especially on somewhat longer timelines. Right now, a lot of the scaling we've seen has come from spending more money on compute, not just from chips getting cheaper. Companies have gone from spending tens of millions on a training run to hundreds of millions to billions. Some of that is just buying a larger share of existing chip production, plus TSMC and others expanding their leading-edge capacity.

But at some point, if you keep scaling spending by something like 3x a year, you run into the fact that AI is already a big share of leading-edge logic production, and you can't just conjure new fabs. A new fab takes several years to build, costs tens of billions of dollars, and depends on bottlenecks like EUV lithography machines from ASML, which has limited production capacity of its own. There's also advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory, which have arguably been tighter bottlenecks recently than the logic dies themselves.

So my rough picture is this. Over the next few years, you can keep scaling compute pretty aggressively by reallocating existing capacity toward AI and by the fab expansions already in the pipeline. Then, maybe around the end of the decade, you'd expect the growth rate of compute to slow somewhat, unless the industry has already committed to a big buildout. In that case, hardware growth becomes limited more by how fast you can grow the semiconductor supply chain, which is maybe something like doubling every couple of years at best, rather than the faster rates we've seen from just spending more.

There are a few important caveats, though. First, algorithmic progress doesn't depend on fabs in the same way. Historically, it's been a comparable contributor to effective compute, so even if hardware scaling slows, you'd still have substantial progress from better algorithms, better data, and better post-training. Second, and I think this is the key thing, if AI gets good enough to substantially automate AI research itself before the hardware wall really bites, then fab limits matter much less for the trajectory. You could get a lot of progress from software improvements on a roughly fixed compute stock. So in some sense the question is whether we reach something like automated AI R&D before compute growth slows. If we do, things could move very fast regardless. If we don't, then fab constraints probably stretch out timelines meaningfully.

The other thing I'd flag is that fab constraints aren't really fixed. If it becomes clear that AI is enormously economically valuable, you'd expect massive investment and possibly government involvement to expand capacity. Fabs take years, but people can parallelize a lot when there's enough money. So I'd think of it less as a hard ceiling and more as something that slows growth from maybe 4-5x a year in compute to something lower for a while, until the supply chain catches up.

r001.rationale: The response says compute can keep scaling for the next few years using existing capacity and planned fab expansions, so hardware can continue advancing AI despite limits on new fab construction.

r002.rationale: It describes compute investment as driving scaling and discusses algorithmic progress separately, but does not say increased compute investment drives algorithmic development.

r003.rationale: It predicts fab constraints may slow hardware growth and stretch timelines, while saying algorithmic progress is less dependent on fabs; it does not predict that fab constraints slow algorithmic development.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to understand is that fab buildout is already the main physical bottleneck on compute scaling, and it operates on pretty long timescales. A new leading-edge fab takes something like three to five years to go from breaking ground to meaningful output, and TSMC's expansion plans are basically set years in advance. So if you imposed limits today, you wouldn't actually see much effect on what gets trained in the next two or three years, because that compute is already baked in — the fabs exist, the wafer allocations are mostly spoken for, and the GPUs are being shipped.

Where it bites is further out. The current trajectory has something like a 4x or 5x per year increase in training compute for frontier runs, and a big fraction of that is just more chips rather than better chips per dollar. If you cap fab construction, you're capping the "more chips" part. So my rough picture is that the trajectory looks basically unchanged through maybe 2027 or 2028, and then it starts to diverge, potentially quite substantially, because you've removed the thing that was supposed to supply the next couple orders of magnitude.

Now, how much that matters for AI progress depends a lot on your model of where the progress is coming from. If you think we're mostly compute-constrained — that the algorithms are good enough and we just need to scale — then fab limits are a very big deal, they could plausibly add years to timelines. If you think a lot of the action is in algorithmic efficiency, which has historically been giving you something like 2x or 3x per year on its own, then you're slowing things down but not stopping them, because labs would just shift effort toward squeezing more out of fixed hardware. My guess is it's somewhere in between, and I'd lean toward compute mattering a lot, so I'd expect a real slowdown but not a halt.

There's also a weird dynamic where constraints on new fabs make existing compute more valuable, which concentrates power in whoever already has it. So it's not obviously good from a governance standpoint — you might be freezing the current distribution of capabilities in place rather than slowing everyone uniformly. And of course there's the question of whether limits actually hold internationally; if the US restricts and China doesn't, or vice versa, that's a very different world from a coordinated slowdown.

One more thing I'd flag: I think people sometimes imagine the point of fab limits is to directly prevent some specific dangerous training run. I don't think that's realistic given the lag times. The more plausible story is that it buys time at the margin — a year or two on the back end — during which you might get better alignment techniques, better evals, better institutions. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much you value that time and how confident you are it'd actually be used well.

r001.rationale: The response says fab limits cap the supply of more chips and that labs may improve efficiency on fixed hardware, but it does not clearly state that hardware improvements can continue advancing AI under those constraints.

r002.rationale: It discusses compute scaling and historical algorithmic efficiency gains, but does not identify increased compute investment as a driver of algorithmic development.

r003.rationale: It predicts a slowdown in AI progress from fab limits, while suggesting labs may shift effort toward algorithmic efficiency; it does not predict slower algorithmic development.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s more likely to slow things down than to impose a hard ceiling. There’s a distinction between how much compute you need to train a more capable model and how much you need to run lots of copies of that model. You can concentrate a relatively small fraction of the world’s chips on a training run, whereas deploying AI across a large fraction of the economy could require considerably more hardware.

So if AI capabilities improve quickly, you could get into a situation where you have very capable systems, but you can’t manufacture enough chips to run as many of them as you’d like. Building new fabs takes time, and even if AI makes the design and planning much easier, you still have to construct the buildings and produce the equipment.

But there are several ways to make progress without building new fabs. You can allocate more existing manufacturing capacity to AI chips, use the chips you have more efficiently, or improve the algorithms so that you get more useful work per unit of compute. And if the AI systems themselves can do research, that last route could be quite important.

So I wouldn’t expect fab construction to reliably prevent very powerful AI. I’d expect it to matter more for how quickly you can scale up the number of systems you’re running, and therefore how quickly some of the economic effects happen.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can progress through using existing chips more efficiently and improving algorithms, but it does not state that hardware improvements themselves can advance AI under fab construction constraints.

r002.rationale: It mentions allocating existing manufacturing capacity to AI chips, but does not identify increased compute investment as a driver of algorithmic development.

r003.rationale: It predicts that fab constraints can slow AI scaling and economic effects, but does not say they will slow algorithmic development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between increasing the amount of compute used for a single training run and increasing the total amount of compute available. You can make a training run much bigger by spending more money and allocating a larger fraction of existing chip production to it, without needing the world to build dramatically more fabs.

So I wouldn’t expect limits on building fabs to be a hard constraint on AI progress in the near term. There are other potential bottlenecks, like power, putting together very large clusters, and getting those clusters to work reliably. And you can also make progress through better algorithms without increasing the amount of hardware.

Fab capacity could become much more important if there’s demand to run enormous numbers of AI systems — particularly if those systems can do economically valuable work and there’s a strong incentive to deploy as many as possible. At that point, you might want to expand chip production much faster than you physically can. That could substantially slow the expansion of AI’s economic impact, even if it doesn’t prevent you from training a more capable system.

There’s uncertainty about when those constraints bite. But I’d be cautious about going from ‘fabs take a long time to build’ to ‘therefore AI capabilities can’t advance very quickly.’ Those are different claims.

r001.rationale: The response says existing chip production can support larger training runs and that algorithms can improve without more hardware. It does not state that hardware improvements can continue advancing AI under fab constraints.

r002.rationale: It mentions spending more money to make a training run larger, then separately says algorithms can improve without more hardware. It does not identify increased compute investment as a driver of algorithmic development.

r003.rationale: The response says fab limits could slow the expansion of AI’s economic impact, while distinguishing that from training more capable systems. It does not predict that fab constraints will slow algorithmic development.
